result:
A few things worth checking before Friday, roughly in priority order:

**Audit trail / legal defensibility** — "legally binding" on their marketing page isn't the same as your legal/compliance team confirming what's actually in the certificate. For a dispute to hold up, you need to know it captures signer identity verification method, IP/timestamp, consent-to-sign language, and ideally a hash that lets you prove the PDF wasn't altered *independent of SignFast* (i.e., if they go under or you're mid-litigation and can't reach them, can you still verify it yourself?). Worth a 15-minute call with legal, not just sales.

**Demo ≠ production edge cases** — two clean demo runs don't exercise: partial/abandoned signing sessions, signer declines, expired links, malformed webhook payloads, or duplicate webhook deliveries. If your completed-document pull relies on webhooks, make sure you have idempotency and a reconciliation job (poll their API periodically to catch anything a missed webhook would've dropped), not just fire-and-forget.

**Uptime stat is the wrong metric** — 99.98% is their status-page uptime, not a guarantee your onboarding webhook fires reliably or that mid-signature-flow failures are rare. Ask what happens to a customer who's mid-signature when SignFast has an incident — does the session recover, or does the customer have to restart?

**Data handling** — confirm there's a signed DPA, and check what customer PII (SSNs, etc., if any) flows through their widget vs. stays client-side.

**Rollback path** — given the Friday timeline, I'd run old and new processes in parallel for the first batch of real customers rather than a hard cutover, so a bad edge case doesn't block onboarding entirely.

None of this should blow up the Friday date if the integration itself is solid — it's mostly a half-day of verification (docs + one legal conversation) rather than rework. Happy to look at the actual webhook/API integration code if you want a second set of eyes there.
